paragraphs: AlphaVerus addresses a gap between generating plausible code and generating code whose correctness can be mathematically checked. Formal verification offers such checks, but language models face scarce training examples and difficult proof requirements. The paper approaches this problem by translating programs from a language with more available resources and using a verifier to guide successive improvements.

The framework has three phases. It explores candidate translations, refines them with a tree search procedure called Treefinement, and filters programs whose specifications do not match their intended task. Verifier feedback guides refinement. The filtering step addresses reward hacking: satisfying a verification target is not sufficient if that target has drifted away from the requested program.

Through this iterative process, AlphaVerus enables LLaMA-3.1-70B to produce verified code without human intervention or model fine-tuning. The authors demonstrate verified solutions for HumanEval and MBPP. These findings support a route toward more trustworthy code generation in which translation, search, and specification checks work together, with correctness tied to the formal requirements being verified.
icml-2025-alphaverus-bootstrapping-forma.tldr: AlphaVerus combines program translation, verifier-guided tree search, and specification filtering to generate formally verified code without model fine-tuning.

paragraphs: Comparing point clouds requires deciding which differences reflect shape and which merely reflect orientation. Procrustes-Wasserstein addresses this by making comparisons invariant to transformations such as rotations and reflections. The paper strengthens its mathematical foundations by constructing a space of discrete probability measures on which Procrustes-Wasserstein satisfies the requirements of a distance.

The authors also extend the computational framework. They investigate several ways to initialize existing Procrustes-Wasserstein algorithms, then define a corresponding barycenter and give an algorithm for estimating it. A barycenter serves as a representative shape for a collection of point clouds. Accounting for alignment within this construction matters when the desired representative should retain geometric structure despite differently oriented inputs.

Benchmarks against existing optimal transport approaches show better performance in scenarios requiring accurate alignment and shape preservation. An archaeological application further demonstrates the usefulness of these representative shapes. The contribution therefore connects a mathematical justification for the distance with practical methods for comparing and summarizing point clouds, with potential applications to both two-dimensional and three-dimensional shape analysis.
icml-2025-an-in-depth-look-at-the-procru.tldr: The paper establishes Procrustes-Wasserstein as a distance on a constructed space and develops barycenters for representative, well-aligned point-cloud shapes.

paragraphs: Attention determines how tokens influence one another as their representations pass through transformer layers. This paper asks what happens to those representations asymptotically: what behavior emerges as the propagation process continues toward its limiting regime? The focus is a mathematical account of attention's long-term behavior, connecting the mechanism's interactions to the eventual relationship among tokens.

The authors establish several results under different assumptions. Across those results, token representations converge toward one another, producing a form of consensus. This gives theoretical support to a phenomenon previously observed empirically. The assumptions remain part of each result: the shared conclusion describes the analyzed settings rather than establishing that every finite transformer computation must make all tokens identical.

The paper compares its findings with earlier theoretical work and illustrates them through simulations and experiments involving GPT-2. Together, these elements connect limiting mathematical behavior with observations in a language model. The significance is a clearer account of how attention can progressively reduce differences among token representations, and a framework for interpreting the convergence observed in the studied systems.
icml-2025-consensus-is-all-you-get-the-r.tldr: Under several analyzed sets of assumptions, attention makes token representations converge toward one another asymptotically.

paragraphs: Offline learning from human preferences trains a policy using an existing collection of inputs, sampled responses, and comparisons between those responses. Several prominent language-model alignment methods follow this pattern, but they make different design choices. This paper studies how those choices affect the quality of the resulting policy through a unified theoretical analysis.

The analysis considers methods including DPO, IPO, and SLiC. It examines the loss function, the policy used to normalize response log-likelihoods, and the policy that originally sampled the training responses. These are distinct parts of the learning setup: they shape how preferences become an optimization objective and which responses are available as evidence. The framework makes their roles accessible within one treatment.

The authors avoid relying on the standard reparameterization arguments used to motivate some methods, allowing their analysis to cover a broader family. A small experiment on a summarization benchmark checks some of the theoretical findings. The contribution is therefore guidance for understanding alignment design choices, supported by a limited empirical check rather than a claim that one method universally dominates.
icml-2025-design-considerations-in-offli.tldr: A unified theoretical analysis explains how losses, normalization policies, and data-sampling policies affect offline preference learning.

paragraphs: EnIGMA studies how tool interfaces affect a language-model agent's ability to solve cybersecurity Capture The Flag challenges autonomously. These challenges require finding and exploiting vulnerabilities. The paper focuses on interactive terminal programs, where progress depends on operating a utility through an ongoing exchange with the environment.

The authors introduce Interactive Agent Tools that let the agent use utilities such as a debugger and a server connection tool. This gives the agent access to interactions that are important for solving the challenges. Across 390 challenges drawn from four benchmarks, the tools and interfaces substantially improve performance. EnIGMA achieves reported state-of-the-art results on NYU CTF, Intercode-CTF, and CyBench.

The study also examines the reliability of evaluating such agents. It develops methods to quantify data leakage and identifies a behavior called soliloquizing: the model invents observations without actually interacting with the environment. This finding highlights a concrete distinction between an agent's generated account of events and evidence obtained through its tools. The paper combines stronger challenge-solving performance with closer scrutiny of how that performance is assessed.
icml-2025-enigma-interactive-tools-subst.tldr: EnIGMA improves autonomous CTF solving through interactive tools while analyzing data leakage and fabricated environment observations.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model across separate clients, but those clients can differ in both their data and their computing workloads. These differences can produce inconsistent updates and weaken the final model. FedECADO approaches the coordination problem by representing federated learning as a dynamical system, providing a basis for handling both sources of heterogeneity.

For differences in data distribution, FedECADO uses an aggregate sensitivity model that reflects how much data each client processes. For differences in computing, it introduces a multi-rate integration method with adaptive step sizes. This method synchronizes updates from active clients in continuous time. The two components address related but distinct issues: how client data influences aggregation and how updates produced at differing rates are coordinated.

The authors compare FedECADO with FedProx, FedExp, and FedNova and report higher classification accuracy across numerous heterogeneous scenarios. These findings support the usefulness of treating client coordination as a dynamical-system problem. The demonstrated benefit concerns the evaluated settings with differing data distributions and workloads, where the algorithm's aggregation and timing mechanisms are intended to work together.
icml-2025-fedecado-a-dynamical-system-mo.tldr: FedECADO uses a dynamical-system formulation to coordinate clients with differing data and computing workloads, improving accuracy in evaluated heterogeneous settings.

paragraphs: Protein language models learn from large collections of protein sequences and can predict properties of protein structure and function. However, the internal features supporting those predictions are poorly understood. This paper trains sparse autoencoders on the residual stream of ESM-2 to extract features that can be examined for biological meaning.

By characterizing those features, the authors find that the model represents proteins using both broadly shared features and features specific to particular protein families. They also use linear probes on the autoencoder features to identify known sequence determinants of thermostability and subcellular localization. This links elements of the model's internal representation to recognizable biological properties rather than considering predictive performance alone.

Some predictive features lack known functional associations. The authors propose hypotheses about their possible biological roles and provide visualization tools to support interpretation. Those proposed roles remain hypotheses, which is central to the paper's aim of using model analysis to guide biological investigation. The work also examines limitations of protein language models and releases code, weights, and a feature visualizer.
icml-2025-from-mechanistic-interpretabil.tldr: Sparse autoencoders reveal biologically interpretable features in ESM-2 and help generate hypotheses about protein mechanisms.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization uses an acquisition function to decide which evaluation to perform next. That choice strongly affects how efficiently the optimizer uses its evaluations, but effective acquisition functions can vary across problems. FunBO addresses the design of these decision rules by using a language model to discover acquisition functions expressed as computer code.

Built on FunSearch, the method learns from access to evaluations on a limited collection of objective functions. The resulting acquisition functions are also provided as analytic expressions, making the discovered rules explicit. The authors assess them on global optimization benchmarks and hyperparameter optimization tasks, testing whether rules discovered from a restricted training collection remain useful across other settings.

The reported functions generalize both within and outside the training distribution of objectives. In the evaluations, they outperform established general-purpose acquisition functions and compete with functions customized to particular problem types through transfer learning. The findings support automated discovery as a way to obtain broadly effective optimization rules, while retaining the qualified distinction between outperforming general-purpose methods and matching more specialized alternatives.
icml-2025-funbo-discovering-acquisition-.tldr: FunBO uses language-model-guided discovery to create acquisition functions that generalize across evaluated Bayesian optimization problems.

paragraphs: Adapting a pretrained 3D vision model by updating all its parameters can require substantial computation and storage. Parameter-efficient methods reduce that burden, but prompting based mainly on input tokens can struggle to capture point-cloud geometry. GAPrompt makes geometric information an explicit part of adaptation, aiming to retain strong performance while training a small fraction of parameters.

The method combines three components. A Point Prompt accompanies the original point cloud and guides attention to fine geometric details. A Point Shift Prompter extracts information about overall shape and enables geometric adjustments tailored to each input. Prompt Propagation then brings that shape information into the model's feature extraction process. Together, these components connect local detail, global shape, and internal representation.

Across the reported benchmarks, GAPrompt significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods and achieves results competitive with full fine-tuning. It does so using only 2.19% trainable parameters. The finding supports geometry-aware adaptation as a way to improve the performance-efficiency trade-off for pretrained 3D models, with both input-level adjustments and propagated shape information contributing to the proposed design.
icml-2025-gaprompt-geometry-aware-point-.tldr: GAPrompt incorporates local and global point-cloud geometry into efficient adaptation, achieving competitive results with only 2.19% trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Schedule-free optimization methods have shown strong empirical results in neural-network training, motivating a theoretical question: how effective are they when the objective is nonconvex? This paper proves that schedule-free SGD achieves optimal iteration complexity for nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization problems. The claim concerns the number of iterations required in the analyzed optimization setting.

The proof comes from a broader framework that turns online learning algorithms into algorithms for optimizing nonconvex losses. The framework recovers existing conversion methods and produces two new ones. One of those new conversions corresponds directly to schedule-free SGD, connecting the practical method to the theory needed to establish its optimality.

The analysis also gives insight into choosing schedule-free SGD's parameters, addressing behavior that convex theory does not explain. Its contribution is therefore both a result about a particular optimizer and a general construction for developing nonconvex optimization algorithms. The stated optimality is an iteration-complexity guarantee; the paper's motivation comes from empirical training success, while its main finding provides a theoretical foundation for that method in a broader class of objectives.
icml-2025-general-framework-for-online-t.tldr: A general online-to-nonconvex conversion framework establishes optimal iteration complexity for schedule-free SGD in nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization.

paragraphs: Data pruning selects a small representative subset to reduce the cost of training on a large dataset. Noise makes this selection harder, especially when a method relies on the empirical mean, which can be strongly influenced by outliers. GM Matching replaces that vulnerable target with the geometric median, a robust estimator with a breakdown point of one half.

The method iteratively chooses a subset of k examples whose mean approximates the geometric median of the potentially corrupted dataset. The distinction between target and subset is useful: the selected subset still has a mean, but that mean is matched to a robust reference. The authors prove an O(1/k) convergence rate, improving on uniform sampling's O(1/√k) rate, including in their analysis of arbitrary corruption.

Experiments on image classification and image generation show consistent improvements over the compared pruning approaches, particularly at high corruption rates. The result connects robustness in the selection target with practical performance on noisy data. The geometric median's stated breakdown point also matters when interpreting robustness; arbitrary corruption does not imply tolerance of an unrestricted corrupted fraction.
icml-2025-geometric-median-gm-matching-f.tldr: GM Matching selects subsets whose means approximate a geometric median, improving theoretical convergence and empirical pruning performance on noisy data.

paragraphs: Grokking describes a transition from memorizing training examples to generalizing their underlying logical structure. Earlier studies largely examined small synthetic tasks. This paper extends the idea to factual reasoning with real-world knowledge graphs, where sparse knowledge can make it difficult for transformers to learn how to combine facts across multiple steps.

The authors add carefully designed synthetic data to increase the ratio of inferred facts to atomic facts beyond the threshold required for grokking. They find that even factually incorrect synthetic examples can improve the emerging reasoning circuits in their setting. Their explanation is that these examples encourage reliance on relationships and structure rather than memorization. An internal analysis examines how increasing the ratio promotes generalizing circuits.

On 2WikiMultiHopQA, the approach reaches reported accuracies of up to 95–100%, substantially improving on strong baselines and matching or exceeding reported state-of-the-art results. These findings suggest that structured augmentation can help unlock implicit multi-hop reasoning. The observation about incorrect examples is tied to this designed augmentation process; the contribution is evidence about learning relational structure from the constructed data.
icml-2025-grokking-in-the-wild-data-augm.tldr: Structured synthetic augmentation promotes grokking on real-world factual data and yields strong reported multi-hop reasoning accuracy.

paragraphs: An image inverse problem asks which plausible original images could have produced a corrupted observation. A generative model can guide reconstruction toward natural-looking solutions, but conditioning a diffusion model on an observation is challenging because generation proceeds sequentially. When diffusion takes place in an autoencoder's latent space, the transformations between latent representations and images introduce further difficulties.

LD-SMC addresses these issues with sequential Monte Carlo sampling in latent space. The authors define a generative model that includes additional auxiliary observations, then perform posterior inference using a backward diffusion process. This formulation places the reconstruction task within a sampling procedure that accounts for observations while following the model's sequential generation structure.

Evaluations on ImageNet and FFHQ show benefits over competing methods across several inverse problems, with especially strong findings for challenging inpainting tasks. The practical significance is a method for obtaining plausible reconstructions while handling the extra complications of latent diffusion. The evidence supports the proposed inference procedure on the evaluated reconstruction tasks, particularly where missing image content makes conditioning difficult.
icml-2025-inverse-problem-sampling-in-la.tldr: LD-SMC combines latent diffusion with sequential Monte Carlo inference to improve image reconstruction, especially on challenging inpainting tasks.

paragraphs: Software development often requires modifying existing code according to varied instructions. NextCoder addresses this capability through both training data and model adaptation. Its synthetic-data pipeline starts from seed programs and editing criteria, producing original code, modified code, and instructions that vary in wording style and level of detail.

The adaptation algorithm, SeleKT, aims to improve editing while retaining abilities already present in the base model. It first uses a dense gradient-based step to identify weights important for editing, then applies a sparse projection onto the base model to avoid overfitting. This design makes preservation of existing capabilities part of the adaptation procedure, alongside learning the new task.

NextCoder models adapted from QwenCoder-2.5 perform strongly on five editing benchmarks, surpassing comparable-size models and several larger ones. The authors also test their approach with DeepSeekCoder and QwenCoder, compare it with other fine-tuning methods, and show retention of code generation and general problem-solving abilities. These results support the combination of diverse synthetic edits and selective adaptation, with models, data, and implementation released for reuse.
icml-2025-nextcoder-robust-adaptation-of.tldr: NextCoder combines diverse synthetic editing data with selective adaptation to improve code edits while retaining broader coding abilities.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents need useful representations of their environment, particularly when raw observations are high-dimensional or unstructured. Laplacian-based methods derive features from the graph describing transitions between states. Specifically, they use eigenvectors of its Laplacian matrix to encode structure that can support learning and transfer across tasks.

This paper asks whether those representations can be learned online alongside policy learning, with theoretical guarantees. The authors formulate the task as online optimization using the Asymmetric Graph Drawing Objective. They analyze online projected gradient descent and establish convergence under assumptions described as mild. The guarantee therefore depends on the conditions of that analysis rather than applying to every possible learning process.

Simulation studies empirically support convergence to the true Laplacian representation. The paper also investigates how different reinforcement-learning algorithms fit with online representation learning. This matters because an agent's representation and policy can develop together during interaction, making their compatibility part of the design problem. The contribution combines an online learning formulation, a conditional convergence analysis, and empirical evidence about the resulting representation.
icml-2025-online-laplacian-based-represe.tldr: The paper develops online Laplacian representation learning alongside policy learning and proves convergence under stated assumptions.

paragraphs: A fair Bayes optimal classifier seeks the best accuracy available on a distribution while satisfying a fairness constraint. This paper investigates how its accuracy responds when an adversary perturbs that distribution. Existing robustness guarantees for an unconstrained deterministic optimal classifier can fail once fairness constraints are imposed.

The authors show that allowing randomized predictions restores robustness of the optimal fair classifier's accuracy to malicious distribution noise. Their result covers Demographic Parity, Equal Opportunity, and Predictive Equality. The central distinction concerns accuracy under perturbation: deterministic fair optimization can lose a robustness property that is available to the randomized formulation.

The paper also reports accuracy and efficiency benefits from randomization and shows that the randomized fair optimal classifier can be nearly deterministic, randomizing on at most one data point. Thus, the theoretical benefits do not require randomness throughout its predictions. The result makes a case for treating a small amount of randomization as a meaningful design choice when seeking accurate fair classifiers whose optimal accuracy remains robust to adversarial changes in the data distribution.
icml-2025-optimal-fair-learning-robust-t.tldr: Randomization restores accuracy robustness for fair Bayes optimal classifiers under adversarial distribution noise, while requiring randomness at at most one data point.

paragraphs: This paper studies systems that evolve continuously but are measured by sensors at irregular discrete times. Choosing when to measure involves more than estimation accuracy: frequent measurements can consume energy or generate heat, and accuracy can depend on sensor or target motion. The authors model these interacting effects through an auxiliary state-space system.

Measurement arrivals are assumed to follow independent Poisson processes with a separate rate for each sensor. Under this formulation, the authors derive an upper bound on the Kalman filter's mean posterior covariance along the mean auxiliary state. The bound varies smoothly with measurement rates, enabling gradient-based optimization of a quantity that reflects estimation uncertainty.

A finite-horizon optimal control framework jointly chooses measurement rates and auxiliary-state dynamics while accounting for costs and constraints. A further deterministic procedure converts the optimized rates into actual measurement times. Experiments in state-space filtering and dynamic temporal Gaussian process regression show improved trade-offs between resource use and estimation accuracy. The approach therefore links a tractable uncertainty bound to both sensing decisions and the physical processes that influence their cost.
icml-2025-optimal-sensor-scheduling-and-.tldr: A differentiable uncertainty bound enables joint optimization of sensor measurement rates and auxiliary dynamics, improving evaluated resource-accuracy trade-offs.

paragraphs: Otter tackles writing tests from a software issue before a patch exists. The goal is to create a test that can validate a future fix, using the issue as the starting point. This supports test-driven development and provides a way to assess patches produced by software-engineering agents.

The paper introduces TDD-Bench-Verified to evaluate this task and presents Otter as a language-model-based solution. Otter combines generated outputs with rule-based analysis that checks and repairs them. It also uses a self-reflective action planner. Together, these components address the process of producing a usable test from an issue, including examining and correcting the system's own outputs.

Experiments show that Otter outperforms the compared state-of-the-art systems for generating tests from issues. It also improves systems that generate patches from issues. These findings make issue-based testing useful both as a standalone development aid and as part of an automated repair workflow. The stated results concern test generation and patch-system improvements; greater developer productivity and more robust code are the broader goals motivating the work.
icml-2025-otter-generating-tests-from-is.tldr: Otter generates tests from software issues before patches exist, improving evaluated test-generation and patch-generation systems.

paragraphs: Language-model capacity involves both the number of parameters and the computation performed for each example. These usually increase together, making their separate contributions difficult to understand. Sparse mixture-of-experts models provide a way to investigate the relationship because they can add parameters without proportionally increasing the computation used for each example.

The paper varies sparsity, defined as the proportion of total parameters that are inactive, and studies effects on pretraining and downstream performance. It examines this choice under constraints such as model parameter size and total training compute. This framing makes sparsity a resource-allocation decision: how much model capacity should exist, and how much should participate in processing an example?

The authors find an optimal sparsity level under the constraints they investigate, improving both training efficiency and model performance. The result does not prescribe one universal sparsity setting; the relevant optimum depends on the resource constraints. By examining parameters and computation together, the work adds sparsity to the scaling-law picture and offers evidence for designing mixture-of-experts architectures around a specific budget.
icml-2025-parameters-vs-flops-scaling-la.tldr: The study finds constraint-dependent optimal sparsity levels that improve mixture-of-experts language-model efficiency and performance.

paragraphs: A zero-shot reinforcement-learning agent should reuse its exploration of an environment to solve new tasks without further interaction. Proto Successor Measure addresses this by representing the space of possible behaviors before a particular reward is supplied. Behaviors are expressed through visitation distributions, which describe how an agent occupies the environment.

The authors prove that every possible behavior can be expressed as an affine combination of policy-independent basis functions. This gives a common representation across policies. Once a reward function is provided, the remaining task is to choose combination weights corresponding to an optimal policy. The theorem separates the representation of possible behavior from the later choice of which behavior a reward makes desirable.

The paper derives a practical algorithm that learns these basis functions from reward-free interaction data. It shows that the approach can produce a near-optimal policy for a supplied reward without collecting additional environmental interactions. The distinction between the exact representational result and the practical near-optimal outcome matters: the basis describes the behavior space, while the learning algorithm makes that representation usable for downstream tasks in the explored environment.
icml-2025-proto-successor-measure-repres.tldr: Proto Successor Measure represents behaviors with shared basis functions, enabling near-optimal reward-specific policies without further environment interaction.

paragraphs: Training data often combines several domains, and changing their relative weights can substantially change downstream performance. Soup-of-Experts aims to produce a model suited to a requested domain mixture without retraining for each request. The architecture stores a bank of expert parameters and combines them linearly to instantiate one model.

The combination coefficients are learned as a function of the requested domain weights. During training, the system samples a random mixture, constructs the corresponding model, and backpropagates through a batch sampled according to that same mixture. This connects the desired data composition to the parameters of the resulting model, training the architecture to support different specialization choices.

The authors demonstrate rapid creation of small specialist models on several language-modeling tasks. At test time, the architecture can instantiate a model for any supplied domain weights with minimal computational cost and no retraining. Its stated appeal is strongest when many specialist models must be delivered quickly under a size constraint. The contribution is a reusable parameter bank that supports inexpensive construction of models tailored to different domain mixtures.
icml-2025-soup-of-experts-pretraining-sp.tldr: Soup-of-Experts learns to combine expert parameters into small specialist models for requested domain mixtures without retraining.

paragraphs: The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis suggests that a dense network contains sparse configurations that can match its generalization with far fewer parameters. Finding such a configuration is expensive, and a discovered sparsity mask does not readily transfer to new random initial weights. This paper investigates whether alignment between optimization solutions explains that transfer difficulty.

The authors build on work suggesting that networks trained from different random initializations can reach solutions in the same loss basin after permuting their components. They hypothesize that an existing lottery-ticket mask is misaligned with the basin associated with a new initialization. Their proposed remedy is to permute the mask to align it before sparse training from that new starting point.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet, using VGG11 and ResNet20/50, show significantly better generalization with permuted masks than with unchanged lottery-ticket masks. This supports alignment as a useful practical consideration when reusing sparse structures. The explanation about basin misalignment remains a hypothesis, while the demonstrated finding is the empirical improvement obtained by permuting the mask across the tested datasets and models.
icml-2025-sparse-training-from-random-in.tldr: Permuting lottery-ticket masks to align with new random initializations improves sparse-training generalization in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Long sequences make transformer inference expensive because self-attention has quadratic complexity. Star Attention addresses this cost with a block-sparse approximation distributed across multiple hosts. Its design uses two phases so that context processing can happen in parallel while later query and response tokens retain access to the preceding sequence.

In the first phase, hosts process blocks of context with local attention. In the second, query and response tokens use global attention over all previously cached tokens. This division is the central mechanism: the initial context is handled with restricted interactions, followed by sequence-wide access during query and response processing. The method also aims to keep communication between hosts low.

The authors report reductions in memory requirements and inference time of up to elevenfold while preserving 97–100% of accuracy. Star Attention is designed to integrate with most transformer language models trained using global attention. These findings support a substantial efficiency benefit from the approximation in the evaluated settings, with the reported accuracy retention describing the empirical trade-off rather than an exact equivalence to full attention.
icml-2025-star-attention-efficient-llm-i.tldr: Star Attention combines parallel local context processing with global query attention, reporting up to elevenfold efficiency gains while retaining 97–100% of accuracy.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model adapt to a task from examples in its input. This paper examines that ability for sequence-to-sequence tasks using a formal structured language pair. Except for very short inputs, the studied models fail to learn consistently across all output positions, revealing difficulty in aligning input elements with their corresponding outputs.

The authors connect this alignment problem to incomplete induction heads, mechanisms important for learning new discrete mappings from context. They propose ICA-Tune, a focused fine-tuning procedure that uses in-context examples. Two accuracy probes track the mechanism: alignment emerges in middle layers without direct supervision, followed by an abrupt increase in induction-head completeness in higher layers.

Compared with standard fine-tuning, ICA-Tune produces more sample-efficient learning and better generalization to out-of-distribution instances. The findings connect a specific failure of sequence learning with an internal change accompanying improvement. The formal language-pair setting is central to the evidence, allowing the authors to study alignment and mapping behavior systematically and to test whether targeted fine-tuning addresses the observed weakness.
icml-2025-the-missing-alignment-link-of-.tldr: ICA-Tune improves studied sequence-to-sequence learning by encouraging input-output alignment and more complete induction heads.

paragraphs: Posterior predictive densities support uncertainty quantification and comparisons between inference methods. They are often estimated by averaging Monte Carlo samples. This paper shows that such averages can have extremely low signal-to-noise ratios, making the estimates unreliable even when the underlying posterior inference is exact.

The theoretical analysis identifies three factors that can rapidly worsen the estimator's signal-to-noise ratio: mismatch between training and test data, a larger latent space, and more test data relative to training data. Examples empirically confirm these effects. In some cases, estimates remain wrong by hundreds of nats despite using a million samples, illustrating how a large sample count can coexist with poor estimation.

The authors also explore adaptive importance sampling as a possible mitigation. They learn its proposal distribution by maximizing a variational proxy for signal-to-noise ratio. This is an illustrative response rather than the paper's primary contribution. The main finding separates the quality of posterior inference from the reliability of a predictive-density estimate, showing why accurate inference alone does not remove this particular source of estimation error.
icml-2025-understanding-the-difficulties.tldr: Simple Monte Carlo posterior predictive estimates can be highly unreliable even with exact inference and very large sample counts.
